# Introduction {#sec-chapter-17-introduction .unnumbered}

When we think about the future of AI coding, the first question that comes to mind is what more demanding work models will be able to take on. Yet the choice of model in real development depends on cost, the nature of the data, and the available hardware, as well as performance. For example, work that spans diverse problems and work that repeats requests in the same format call for different capabilities. When working with material that cannot be sent outside, where the model runs also becomes a criterion for choosing it. To understand how models are changing, we therefore need to examine competition in frontier model performance alongside the possibilities of specialized models and models that run on devices.

As the range of available models grows, who operates them also becomes an important question. Downloading publicly available weights and running a model yourself gives you more room to choose its version and execution environment, while making you responsible for managing access permissions and costs, and for handling failures. In particular, expanding a tool used by one person on their own device into a service for multiple users requires deciding which records to share and which actions to allow each person. Choosing a model leads to assessing the conditions needed to keep it running.

Similar choices arise in the development environments that use these models. To connect the process of editing code in an editor, running checks in a remote environment, and reviewing changes made by an agent, tools must be able to pass along the task's goals and current state. This involves considering both the convenience of connecting tools and the need to separate workspaces and execution permissions. What a development environment integrates and what it keeps separate affects how users delegate work to agents and check the results.

These choices do not end when a tool is first adopted. It also matters how much of the rules, working procedures, and progress records accumulated over time can remain in use when moving to another model or development environment. Common formats and protocols can reduce the burden of switching, but suppliers still differ in execution methods and tool distribution channels. This chapter starts with changes in models, then examines the conditions for operating them yourself, the integration of development environments, and the standardization of harnesses and tools. It examines how these new choices change development for individuals and organizations, and what they need to prepare to make use of them.
